articles.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
articles.summary_snippet: For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad. For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler. Continue reading...

articles.summary_snippet: Europe’s future will be fought over at the ballot box and on Ukraine’s frontline. The danger is that the two strongmen ultimately reap the benefits On the facade of Stenbock House, the Estonian prime minister’s neoclassical office building on a hill in Tallinn, sits a plaque commemorating the murder of 10 heads of government. They were all killed by Soviet forces after the USSR’s invasion of Estonia in 1940. For 51 years, Estonia was occupied by its imperial neighbour; for the past 25 years it has lived independently in its shadow. For the politicians and government officials who work at Stenbock House, the plaque is a constant reminder of the risk the small Baltic nation (population 1.4 million) faces from a neighbour 100 times its size. The trustee overseeing the settlement fund, Don Massey, confirmed on Friday that $180m had been distributed to 450 of about 740 survivors, either directly or through their lawyers if they retained legal representation. Massey said he and his staff are working hard to get payments in the rest of the survivors’ hands by the end of the year but are still waiting on hundreds of distribution forms from survivors and their lawyers. articles.title: Fair-weather Silicon Valley pivots away from the right after blue wave: ‘I’m not Maga’

I’m dark, gothic Maga.” On Wednesday, Musk spoke with much less conviction. “I’m not Maga,” he said. “Well, at least I’m not sure what Maga means.” The richest person in the world added he felt “foolish” for spending some $500m to elect Republicans in the midterms. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said at the New York Times’ DealBook conference, adding that he did not have “some sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party”. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism. Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states . Created in a Rio de Janeiro prison in the 1970s as a self-protection group for prisoners, it started out with low-level crimes like muggings and bank robberies. But in the 1980s, the group moved into the cocaine trade, working with Colombian drug cartels and taking on a social leadership role in many of Rio’s marginalized neighborhoods. articles.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
articles.summary_snippet: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. articles.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
articles.summary_snippet: Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. Continue reading...

articles.summary_snippet: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia. The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions. Continue reading...
